Shiny is an R package that turns your analyses into interactive web applications, without requiring web development experience. For practicing scientists and managers, this opens up real possibilities: imagine building an app that lets stakeholders explore water quality trends over time, filter fish species occurrence records by season or location, or see how monitoring outcomes compare across management scenarios – all through a browser, with no R knowledge required on their end.
In this session, we’ll build interactive data apps from scratch using water quality and fish catch data from the Yolo Bypass Fish Monitoring Program. By the end of the core session, you’ll have a working reactive Shiny app and the foundation to start building your own for the group projects.

title: Programmatic Data Access in R
text:
1 Overview
One of the most common reproducibility barriers in data-driven science isn’t in the analysis code itself, but rather in how data gets loaded in the first place. A script full of hardcoded file paths like read_csv("C:/Users/jsmith/Desktop/data_final_v3.csv") might work perfectly on one machine and fail immediately on every other.
Getting data programmatically – directly in your code, from a remote source – solves this problem. In this session, we’ll move from ad-hoc data downloads to systematic, reproducible data access. We’ll learn a caching pattern for downloading files reliably, then use the dataRetrieval package to retrieve and visualize USGS streamflow data from monitoring stations. Along the way, we’ll peek under the hood at how web APIs work.

title: Parallel Computing in R
text: In this lesson, we showed examples of computing tasks that are likely limited by the number of CPU cores that can be applied, and we reviewed the architecture of computers to understand the relationship between CPU processors and cores. Next, we reviewed the way in which traditional for loops in R can be rewritten as functions that are applied to a list serially using lapply, and then how the parallel package mclapply function can be substituted in order to utilize multiple cores on the local computer to speed up computations. We also installed and reviewed the use of the foreach package with the %dopar operator to accomplish a similar parallelization using multiple cores. And finally, we reviewed the use of the furrr::future_map() function as a drop in replacement for map operations using asynchronous futures.

title: Style guide
text:
This page collects suggestions for styling lessons so that they look and behave consistently across the Learning Hub curriculum. The suggestions come from how lessons were styled in recent courses (e.g., the 2026 Delta Synthesis week 3 course), plus some preferences we’d like to standardize. Each suggestion includes a short explanation of why it helps.
This page is complementary to the content guidelines (heading levels, callout types, YAML header) and the structure guide (file and folder organization). These are suggestions, not rules - when a lesson needs something different, use your judgment.

title: Style guide
text:
1 Text case



Use
For
Why




snake_case
File names, folder names, and variable names wherever possible
Avoids spaces and capitals that break across operating systems, URLs, and code. Matches the lesson naming scheme used by {lhCore} (e.g., r_programmatic_data_access.qmd).


kebab-case
Code chunk labels (see below)
Quarto’s cross-reference labels (e.g., fig-, tbl- prefixes) use hyphens, so hyphenated labels stay compatible if a chunk later becomes a cross-referenced figure or table.


Title Case
Lesson titles, headings, and callout titles
Headings are scanned in the sidebar and table of contents; consistent capitalization looks tidier and makes titles easy to distinguish from body text.









Note



Callout titles are essentially headings (they are written with a header line inside the callout), so we suggest Title Case for them too, e.g., ### Remember to End the Preview When Done!.

title: Style guide
text:
2 Learning objectives
Start each lesson with a learning objectives callout (see the content guidelines). Write each objective as an observable action that begins with a verb, completing the sentence “By the end of this lesson, you will be able to…”.

Content-driven lessons (most lessons): choose verbs from Bloom’s Taxonomy, which groups verbs by the depth of understanding they describe.
Setup-style lessons (focused on accomplishing a specific task rather than understanding content): more direct action verbs are fine, e.g., set up, configure, install, define.




Level
Example verbs




Remember
define, list, identify, name


Understand
describe, explain, summarize, classify


Apply
use, apply, create, demonstrate


Analyze
compare, differentiate, examine, organize


Evaluate
assess, justify, critique, choose


Create
design, develop, construct, formulate



Why: verbs like “understand” or “know” can’t be observed or assessed, while verbs like “compare” or “apply” tell the learner (and the instructor) what they should be able to do afterward - and suggest what the exercises should ask of them.
:::{.callout-learning}
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Define the key components of a Shiny application (UI, server, reactivity)
- Apply the three rules for building reactive server outputs
- Compare single-file and two-file app structures
:::

title: Style guide
text:
3 Code chunks

3.1 Functional code chunks

Code that readers should see and run: use a standard chunk with the default echo: true.
Code that needs to run behind the scenes (e.g., loading data from a different source than the one shown in the lesson): use #| echo: false (or #| include: false to hide output as well). Why: it keeps the lesson focused on what you want the reader to learn, while the lesson still renders correctly.



3.2 Code that is shown but not run
There are a few ways to show code without running it. In order of preference:

A plain language fence, e.g., ```r - the best choice. Why: it is simplest, and since it isn’t a chunk at all, there’s no chance it will accidentally execute (or fail) during rendering.
A chunk with #| eval: false (i.e., ```{r} plus the option) - acceptable, and the most common choice in existing lessons. Why it’s second best: it gives you chunk features (labels, code-fold, source-line-numbers) but there is more that can go wrong, e.g., forgetting the option.
An escaped chunk header - only when you need to show the chunk header and footer themselves, e.g., when teaching how to write a chunk. In the lesson source, type the opening fence with doubled braces (as in the example below); Quarto renders them as single braces, so readers see a normal chunk that does not run.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages

library(dplyr)
```


3.3 Chunk labels
Name your chunks with #| label: - yes, please! Use short, descriptive, lowercase, hyphenated labels without spaces. Why: labels appear in the document outline in Positron/RStudio so readers can navigate long lessons, they make rendering errors easier to trace, and they’re required for cross-references.
```{r}
#| label: read-yolo-catch

yolo_catch <- read_csv(yolo_catch_file)
```


3.4 Explaining code: end-of-line comments vs. footnotes
Both work, for different purposes:

End-of-line comments (e.g., mean(foo) ### calculates the mean of foo) travel with the code when readers copy it. Use them for short notes the reader should keep in their own script.
Code annotations / footnotes (mean(foo) # <1> and then a numbered list after the chunk) show a hover note or numbered explanation without cluttering the code. Use them for teaching-oriented explanations that don’t belong in the script. See the content guidelines for the syntax.







Tip



If you highlight lines with #| source-line-numbers:, note that a footnote marker on a line can count as an extra line. If the highlight lands in the wrong place, adjust the range (e.g., use "3-4" instead of "3").




3.5 Long code
For long, finished scripts that readers may want to copy but not read line by line, fold the chunk and give it a summary so readers can expand it on demand:
```{r}
#| label: complete-app
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show complete app.R"
```

title: Style guide
text:
4 Tabsets
Tabsets are great for presenting alternatives that readers choose between, e.g., instructions for different IDEs or different methods for the same task. Why: each reader sees only the path relevant to them, which shortens the lesson.
Be careful with headings inside tabsets. The tab labels are written as headings, and when section numbering is enabled (as it is in our theme), headings within tabsets take part in the numbering and can make the numbering behave unexpectedly. So:

Use headings only to label the tabs, not for additional structure inside a tab.
Mark the tab label headings as unnumbered ({.unnumbered}) so they don’t take part in the section numbering.
Use bold text or lists for any structure needed inside a tab.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Positron {.unnumbered}

Instructions for Positron...

#### RStudio {.unnumbered}

Instructions for RStudio...

:::

PositronRStudio


Instructions for Positron…


Instructions for RStudio…

text:
5 Images
Prefer the Markdown image syntax, ![](path){options}, over the HTML <img src="path"> tag.

Strengths of the Markdown syntax: Quarto options such as fig-alt, fig-align, and .lightbox work, captions and cross-references are available, and the syntax is shorter.
Weaknesses: less control over unusual layouts; for those, a fenced div or a raw HTML block may be needed.
<img> mode: works, but Quarto’s image options (alt text via fig-alt, lightbox, alignment) don’t apply, so accessibility and styling must be managed by hand.

Useful options (use these and others as you see fit):
![](images/shiny_introduction/app-screenshot.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .lightbox fig-alt="Screenshot of the example app showing a sidebar of filters and a time series plot"}








Option
What it does
Why use it




fig-alt="..."
Alternative text describing the image
Accessibility: screen readers read it, and it displays if the image fails to load. Describe what the image shows and why it matters, not just “screenshot”.


.lightbox
Click the image to enlarge it
Helpful for screenshots with small text.


width="70%"
Image width relative to the page
Keeps large images from dominating the page, and scales with the window.


fig-align="center"
Centers the image
Looks more intentional than left-aligned images with white space on the right.



Also remember to keep the image folder name identical to the lesson name (see the structure guide), and to keep image file sizes small.

title: Style guide
text:
6 External links
Mark links to other websites with {.external target="_blank" rel="noopener"}:
[NCEAS](https://www.nceas.ucsb.edu/){.external target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

.external adds a small “leaving this site” icon next to the link, so readers know they’re navigating away.
target="_blank" opens the link in a new tab, leaving the course page easily available.
rel="noopener" is a security measure that stops the new page from being able to access the page that opened it (browsers often add it automatically with target="_blank", but it’s good practice to be explicit).

The course template also sets link-external-newwindow and link-external-icon in _quarto.yml, which apply this behavior to external links site-wide. Adding the explicit attributes is a harmless safeguard, and a way to be sure the behavior is applied to a particular link.

title: Style guide
text:
7 Customizing callouts

7.1 Collapse long callouts
Long callouts (extended code, optional details, solutions) can push the main content far down the page. Collapse them with collapse="true", and consider adding a note in the title to tell readers to click to expand. The callout needs a title (header) for the collapse control to appear.
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
### Complete Code (Click to Expand)

Long code or optional detail goes here.
:::






TipComplete Code (Click to Expand)





Long code or optional detail goes here.









Note



This works for the built-in callouts. As noted in the content guidelines, the collapse option may not respond for the custom callouts (exercise, hint, answer, example).




7.2 Callouts with custom icons
To use your own Font Awesome icon in place of the default callout icon, set icon="false" and include the icon in the callout’s title line:
::: {.callout-warning icon="false"}
### {{< fa rocket >}} Activity: Draft Elevator Pitch

Activity instructions go here.
:::






Warning Activity: Draft Elevator Pitch



Activity instructions go here.


Why: a distinctive icon makes a recurring type of content (e.g., activities, “your turn” prompts) instantly recognizable, without having to define a whole new callout type. Browse the available icons in the Font Awesome catalog.

title: Course rendering
text:
Tips, suggestions, standards, naming conventions, structure for new lessons
See https://cambiotraining.github.io/quarto-course-template/materials/01-render_guidelines.html for an idea of how to organize it
The coreR course structure is a website with a left sidebar to navigate among lessons and a right sidebar to show the contents of the current lesson.

title: Course rendering
text:
1 _quarto.yml
In the course repository, the _quarto.yml contains all the information on how to render the website.

title: Course rendering
text:
2 Lessons
The lesson .qmd files are copied out of the lessons package ({lhLessons} by default) and into the course repository. To maintain some order, a prefix is appended to the lesson names, e.g., s01_r_programming_introduction.qmd.






Warning.Rmd vs .qmd



For consistency, lesson files must be Quarto documents with a .qmd extension and a yaml header containing a title (lessons in the package may also carry categories tags, which search_lessons() can filter on). Older lessons in .Rmd format should be updated.

title: Course rendering
text:
3 Lesson supporting files
Some lessons link to external images, data, or embedded slides. These files are stored in directories named images, data, slides, and resources respectively. For a given lesson, correspondingly named subdirectories will appear in each of these directories, like this (for a lesson s01_r_programming_introduction.qmd):

 <project root>
├──  s01_r_programming_introduction.qmd ### the lesson document
├──  s02_github_introduction.qmd ### etc
├──  data
|   └──  r_programming_introduction
|       └──  dataset1.csv ### filename as called in lesson qmd
├──  images
|   ├──   r_programming_introduction
|   |   ├──  image1.png ### filename as called in lesson qmd
|   |   └──  image2.png ### etc
|   └──  github_introduction
|       ├──  image1.png ### filename as called in lesson qmd
|       └──  image2.png ### etc
├──  slides
|   ├──   r_programming_introduction
|   |   ├──  slides.qmd ### filename as embedded in lesson qmd
|   |   └──  lesson_style.scss ### filename as noted in the slides qmd
|   └──  github_introduction
|       ├──  github_slides.qmd ### filename as called in lesson qmd
|       └──  style.css ### etc
├──  resources
|   └──  r_programming_introduction
|       ├──  references.bib ### filename as called in lesson qmd
|       └──  document.pdf ### etc
└── …

If a lesson does not have supporting files, e.g., no images, then there may not be a corresponding folder (e.g., the github_introduction.qmd lesson above does not have a data folder!)






NoteFile structure in created course vs. in lhLessons package



The file structure inside the lhLessons package is similar except:

the lesson .qmds and supporting files/folders all live in the inst folder inside the package repository
the supporting files folders are all prefaced with lesson_ (e.g., lesson_data, lesson_images, lesson_slides, lesson_resources) - this is because R packages don’t like a folder called data in the inst folder, since it may interact with the data folder in the root.

to render properly, the links inside the lesson .qmd should point to data, images, slides, or resources without the lesson_ prefix

all content inside the supporting folders is copied over to the new course without modification.









NoteFile sizes and naming in supporting content



As noted above, all content inside the supporting folders is copied over to the new course without modification. Please be considerate when designing and organizing the supporting content! This includes paying attention to:

File naming - short but descriptive.
File size - particularly for images, ensure the file is as small as reasonable. This holds true especially for screen captures - these are typically captured at full screen resolution, but are quite readable shrunk down to a coarser resolution which saves a huge amount of space. Use a photo app to shrink them please!

title: Course rendering
text:
4 Extensions and formatting
The look of the course site (banner, fonts, colors, callout styling) is kept separate from the lesson content, in a Quarto extension.

init_course() installs the extension for the chosen template by running quarto add nceas-learning-hub/theme_<template> (e.g., theme_delta), along with quarto-ext/fontawesome for icons. This requires the Quarto command line tool and an internet connection. The extensions are installed into the course’s _extensions folder, not the project root.
The template extension (_extensions/nceas-learning-hub/theme/) contains:

_extension.yml, which sets the default HTML options for the site (light and dark themes, table of contents, numbered sections, code copy on hover, and the title banner) and registers the Lua filter.
theme_light.scss and theme_dark.scss, which control fonts, colors, and callout styling.
banner/, with the banner CSS and logo images used in the title banner at the top of each page.
callout_exercise.lua, a filter that implements the custom exercise/hint/answer/example callouts (see the content guidelines).

The _quarto.yml in the course root refers to the extension (under filters: and format: theme-html:) and holds course-specific settings such as the site title, navbar, and sidebar contents.

To change the styling of a single course, edit the files inside its _extensions folder (or add course-specific CSS/SCSS and reference it from _quarto.yml). Avoid editing the lesson .qmd files for styling purposes, so that lessons can still be updated from the lessons package and checked back in without carrying course-specific formatting. Note that edits to the _extensions copy affect only that course; to change the styling for all future courses, the template extension in its own GitHub repository must be updated.

title: Update lessons
text:
In many cases, an instructor may wish to create a custom course book every time the course is taught, typically with a yyyy-mm- date prefix to the course repo. This allows for course participants to maintain access to the course book exactly as it was taught to them, even years later, even if new versions of the course are entirely different. Other times, an instructor may wish to create a course book that is used every time the course is taught. Each philosophy has pros and cons. But one potential downside in either case is that lessons may become outdated over time. Perhaps a package version breaks old features, or perhaps a newer package supersedes the functionality of an older package.
The update_lessons() function can help with this. The function scans an existing course (or limits itself to a set of lessons dictated by the instructor), and, depending on the selection of the instructor, can replace older lessons with versions from the most up to date version of the lessons package. Optionally, the instructor can also revert a lesson to that from an older version of the lessons package, by providing an optional version number based on the lessons package history.
Note, only lessons whose bare name (no sXX_ prefix, no extension) match those in the lessons repository will be updated. For new lessons, or for lesson files whose name has been modified, no changes or updates will be made.

title: Update lessons
text:
1 Arguments
update_lessons() takes the following arguments:

lessons - a vector of lesson names (bare or with .qmd extension) to update. Default "all" updates all course lessons whose bare names match lessons in the lessons package. If a requested lesson is not found in both the course and the requested version of the lessons package, an error is returned.
pkg - the lessons package (default "lhLessons").
version - the version of the lessons package to pull lessons from, given as a commit hash, tag, version, or date. Default NULL pulls the latest version.
org - the GitHub organization where the lessons package repo lives (default "nceas-learning-hub").

The function installs the requested version of the lessons package from GitHub into a temporary library, prints a warning about overwriting, lists the lessons that will be updated, and asks the instructor to confirm (y/n) before overwriting the course lesson files and their associated folders. If the update is canceled, nothing is changed. Afterwards, the package and version recorded for the updated lessons in metadata_lessons.csv are updated (a warning is given if that file is missing). If any selected lessons are already recorded in metadata_lessons.csv at the version being installed, a warning notes this.

title: Publish the course
text:
Publishing a course website is set up automatically by init_course() (see Set up course infrastructure). When init_course(setup_github = TRUE) (the default) is used, the following steps happen:
After this, the GitHub Actions workflow automatically updates the gh-pages branch whenever changes to course material are pushed to the main branch.
If the course was initialized with setup_github = FALSE, none of these steps are performed. In that case the instructor must connect the project to Git and GitHub manually, e.g., using usethis::use_git() and usethis::use_github(organisation = 'nceas-learning-hub') (note the British spelling of organisation), and set up publishing separately. init_course() will print reminders of any outstanding Git/GitHub steps.

title: Publish the course
section: 1 When the GitHub Action fails: render locally first
text:
1 When the GitHub Action fails: render locally first






Warning



The most common reason the publishing GitHub Action fails is lessons containing functional code (e.g., {r} code chunks) that have not been rendered locally. The GitHub Action does not run the lesson code itself; it relies on the stored results in the _freeze directory.


The course is set to freeze: auto in _quarto.yml, so when a lesson is rendered, its code results are stored in the _freeze directory, and are only re-computed when the lesson source changes. If a lesson with functional code is added or modified and pushed to GitHub without a current set of frozen results, the Action has nothing to use and the build fails.
Before pushing new or modified lessons:

Render the whole project locally (e.g., click Render in the Build tab, or run quarto render in the terminal).
Check that the render completes without errors.
Commit and push the changes, including the updated _freeze directory, along with the lesson files.

The docs folder created by the local render does not need to be committed; it is ignored by Git, and the Action publishes the site to the gh-pages branch itself.

title: Set up course infrastructure
text:
The init_course() function is the first step to creating a course. It creates a new R project for the course, saves some metadata about the course in a .csv (metadata_course.csv) for later reference, installs the Quarto website structure and theme template, and (by default) sets up Git/GitHub and automatic publishing. This function has ten arguments, only the first of which is mandatory:

course_proj is the desired name for the course project repository, and will also drive the course’s eventual home on the interwebs. We recommend a format like yyyy-mm-<course type>, such as 2024-10-coreR or 2024-06-delta. Characters other than letters, numbers, _ and - are replaced with _ (with a warning).
course_org is the GitHub organization (or GH user) where the course project will live. Defaults to "nceas-learning-hub".
course_title is a brief, descriptive title for the course. If left blank, defaults to the same as course_proj.
course_desc is a brief (~ 1 sentence) description of the course content. This is stored in the course metadata but currently not otherwise used. If left blank, defaults to the same as course_title.
course_dates is a text field containing the dates of the course, in whatever format. If left blank, no dates will be recorded.
setup_github (default TRUE) initializes the course as a Git-tracked project, makes an initial commit, creates a GitHub repository named course_proj in the organization course_org, and sets up publishing (see Publish the course). Set to FALSE to skip these steps and handle Git/GitHub yourself.
template selects the stylistic template, which defines the default index page, banner colors, hex logo, etc.: "lh" (default) for Learning Hub; "adc" for Arctic Data Center; "delta" for Delta Stewardship Council; "corer" for coreR.
package is the lessons package that supplies the Quarto structure and index page files. Defaults to "lhLessons"; currently a placeholder for potential future custom lesson packages.
loc is the desired location where the new course will be created. Defaults to the current working directory. The location must not be inside an existing Git repository - this is checked before anything is created, and if it is, init_course() stops with an error. If you are currently working in an existing Git-tracked R project, some options:

Close the current project; this should leave you in the default location for projects you’ve set in RStudio. Then it should be fine to use loc = '.' (default).
Keep the current project open, but set loc = '..' to create the new course one level up, parallel to your current project.
Define some custom location and set loc to that directory.

quiet (default TRUE) controls whether progress and diagnostic messages are shown. Set quiet = FALSE to see details.

The function invisibly returns the full path to the new course project. With the default quiet = TRUE, the new project is activated automatically; with quiet = FALSE the instructor is instead prompted (y/n) whether to open the new project. Either way, the instructor is advised to close the current project and open or activate the new course project directly.
After this step, the course has structure but no lessons. We’ll fix that in the next step!






Warning



The course files will be pulled from the version of {lhLessons} package that the instructor currently has installed. We recommend reinstalling the package (remotes::install_github('nceas-learning-hub/lhLessons')) before running this function to make sure you have the latest version!








ExampleExample






init_course(course_proj = '2024-06-delta', 
            course_title = 'NCEAS coreR for Delta Science Program', 
            course_desc = 'As part of a collaboration between NCEAS and the 
                           Delta Science Program, this course has been adapted 
                           from NCEAS coreR course, an in-person immersion in R 
                           programming for environmental data science.',
            course_dates = 'June 10 - 13, 2024', 
            template = 'delta',
            loc = '..')
With quiet = FALSE, the instructor will see messages outlining the steps and the resulting metadata, and recommended next steps such as:
To render the course book, restart RStudio to activate the Build tab.
Recommended next steps: 
  • Edit the index.qmd to ensure it accurately describes the course
  • Use `search_lessons()` to see the lesson catalog from the lesson package
  • Use `setup_lessons(<lessons>)` to install the lessons in the course

title: Set up course infrastructure
text:
2 What init_course() installs
Course structure is set up internally by init_course() (the helper setup_course_structure() is not exported, so it is not called directly by the instructor). Here’s what gets installed:

metadata_course.csv, holding the course project name, organization, title, description, and dates.
A _quarto.yml file that creates the structure of the course site, populated with course info from the metadata. It contains placeholders (# START SESSIONS, # SESSION_LINKS, # END SESSIONS) where setup_lessons() will later insert the lesson sequence.
An index.qmd file with boilerplate text based on the selected template. This can (and should) be edited to provide specific info on the new course.
An _extensions folder with CSS information and image files to control the appearance of the site according to the selected template, such as the header bar at the top, font faces, sizes, colors…
Other miscellaneous course files from the lessons package (e.g., a 404.qmd).
If setup_github = TRUE: a .gitignore and a .github folder with a GitHub Actions workflow to auto-publish the site whenever a new commit is pushed to GitHub (see Publish the course).


2.1 Editing the index.qmd
Edit this file to your heart’s content. You can modify the title in the YAML header, but leave the rest of the header in place. The text of the page is specific to this course. Some boilerplate text is already in place, but you may wish to edit specific learning objectives, schedule, and details about the course book to reflect the needs of the course.


2.2 Linking to Git and GitHub
With the default setup_github = TRUE, init_course() handles the Git and GitHub setup. This requires that your Git user.name and user.email are already configured (the function stops with an error otherwise), and that you have write privileges to the GitHub organization.
If Git/GitHub are not (fully) set up - e.g., setup_github = FALSE - the function checks and prints reminders such as:
This project does not seem to be a Git repository.  You might want to:
  • Use `usethis::use_git()` to set up your project as a Git-tracked project, and then...
  • Use `usethis::use_github(organisation = 'nceas-learning-hub')` to connect the project with Github!
Follow those directions, answering the prompts after each function call. Don’t overlook the organisation = 'nceas-learning-hub' argument (note the British spelling), otherwise it will be linked to your user account.

title: Set up lessons
text: The {lhCore} package works with the {lhLessons} package to find lessons and copy lesson documentation and auxiliary files (images, slides, datasets) into the course, in an order specified by the instructor, and optionally broken into modules (e.g., by day or by topic). The function to perform this task is setup_lessons(). A supporting function, search_lessons(), helps the instructor find lessons.

title: Set up lessons
text:
1 Finding lessons with search_lessons()
To see all available lessons, simply run search_lessons() with no arguments. The function returns a dataframe containing the location of each lesson file in the locally-installed instance of the {lhLessons} package, the lesson name, and the lesson’s categories (topic tags from the lesson’s YAML header; empty if untagged).






ExampleExample






x <- search_lessons()
head(x)
                                   lesson_file                         lesson                              categories
# 1 <pkg path>/activity_reproducibility_lego.qmd  activity_reproducibility_lego     reproducibility, activity, beginner
# 2 <pkg path>/activity_thinking_preferences.qmd  activity_thinking_preferences     team-science, facilitation, activity, beginner
# 3 <pkg path>/blank_placeholder.qmd              blank_placeholder                 template
...




If the instructor wishes to search for lessons related to a topic, the query argument of search_lessons() allows for partial matching and regex patterns (and multiple strings; lessons matching any of them are returned). The lesson names generally start with a prefix of the overall topic or type of lesson, e.g., git_, github_, r_, rstudio_ for topics, or activity_ or lecture_ for style of lesson.






ExampleExample






x <- search_lessons(query = 'r_')
head(x)
                                   lesson_file                       lesson
# 10 <pkg path>/lecture_github_for_proj_mgmt.qmd lecture_github_for_proj_mgmt
# 13         <pkg path>/r_data_visualization.qmd         r_data_visualization
# 14                  <pkg path>/r_functions.qmd                  r_functions
# 15 <pkg path>/r_geospatial_vector_analysis.qmd r_geospatial_vector_analysis
# 16          <pkg path>/r_git_install_guide.qmd          r_git_install_guide
# 17                   <pkg path>/r_packages.qmd                   r_packages
Note that one of the matches is not about the topic R but the search identified a match of r_ in lecture_github_fo**r_**proj_mgmt… regex can be helpful here, e.g., search for '^r_' to look for an R prefix specifically!




Lessons can also be filtered by topic tags using the tags argument, which is matched against each lesson’s YAML categories. By default a lesson matches if it has any of the given tags; use match = 'all' to require all of them. query and tags can be combined.






ExampleExample






search_lessons(tags = c('beginner', 'r'))                 # either tag
search_lessons(tags = c('beginner', 'r'), match = 'all')  # both tags

title: Set up lessons
section: 2 Setting up a sequence of lessons with setup_lessons
text:
2 Setting up a sequence of lessons with setup_lessons
The instructor can give a sequence of lessons to the setup_lessons() function in several ways, depending on complexity or preference: as a vector of lesson names, as a named vector of lesson names (where the names indicate modules), or a data frame containing columns of module and lesson. Alternately, module names can be supplied as a separate vector via the modules argument (same length as lessons); if both are given, modules takes precedence. Lesson names can be given bare or with the .qmd extension. One work flow would be to use Excel or Google Sheets to organize the lessons by module (e.g., day or broad topic) in order, and save that out as a .csv, then read that in. For a simple course, creating a vector or dataframe (e.g., using tibble::tribble()) directly in R may be quicker.
Sample courses are available in the {lhLessons} package to test the functionality or see the proper format: lhLessons::default_course, based on the October 2024 coreR course (and a shorter lhLessons::example_course, used in the function help examples).






ExampleExample






x <- lhLessons::default_course
head(x)

#   module                        lesson
# 1  Day 1        r_rstudio_server_setup
# 2  Day 1                     git_setup
# 3  Day 1    r_programming_introduction
# 4  Day 1    r_quarto_literate_analysis
# 5  Day 1 activity_reproducibility_lego
# 6  Day 2           github_introduction




Once a lesson dataframe has been created or read in, it can be passed to setup_lessons() easily. A named vector (where element names correspond to module names) works identically to a dataframe (element names can be repeated!). If an unnamed vector is used, lessons will still be sequenced in order, but no modules will be assigned.
When the lesson sequence is put into the setup_lessons() function, R will find the file in the {lhLessons} package and copy it into the current repo, along with all its auxiliary files (from the lesson’s matching images, data, slides, and resources folders, where present), update the _quarto.yml to note the sessions in order, and save a metadata_lessons.csv recording each lesson, its module, and the lessons package and version it came from. The function first asks the instructor to confirm they are in the right course project, and stops with an error listing any requested lessons not found in the package. Note, the lesson names are appended with a prefix to keep them in sequence, e.g., s01_ - this is notable because other functions will recognize lesson files in the course based on this prefix. For example, the first lesson in the default course above would show up in a file called s01_r_rstudio_server_setup.qmd.






ExampleExample






### named vector example:
lesson_vec <- c('Day 1' = 'r_rstudio_server_setup', 
                'Day 1' = 'git_setup', 
                'Day 2' = 'github_introduction')
setup_lessons(lesson_vec)

### tribble example:
lesson_df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~ module,  ~ lesson,
   'Day 1', 'r_rstudio_server_setup',
   'Day 1', 'git_setup',
   'Day 2', 'github_introduction'
)
setup_lessons(lesson_df)
These will result in an identical two-day course.










WarningUsing overwrite = TRUE



If a lesson structure is already in place, setup_lessons() returns an error unless overwrite = TRUE. With overwrite = TRUE, after asking for confirmation, the function permanently deletes the existing lesson files (sXX_*.qmd) and the matching lesson folders in images, data, slides, and resources, replaces the lesson list in _quarto.yml (between the # START SESSIONS and # END SESSIONS markers), and installs the new lessons. Any local edits or customizations to those lessons will be lost, and this cannot be undone. Before overwriting, commit your work to Git and consider running compare_diffs() to see how your lessons differ from the lessons package. If the _quarto.yml is missing the START/END markers, the function stops without deleting anything.

title: Modify or add lessons
text:
Frequently while setting up or teaching a course, the instructor makes edits and changes to lessons or a course. Examples:
All these are easy, but require knowing a bit about how the {lhCore} and {lhLessons} packages work together.

title: Modify or add lessons
text:
1 Modifying an existing lesson

1.1 Edits to the lesson .qmd file
The lesson Quarto document is easy and safe to edit. The instructor can modify the title in the yaml header, but probably should leave the rest of the yaml header well enough alone unless they know what they’re doing (e.g., changing numbering, adding a bibliography, other rendering options).






Tip



See the “Content guidelines” tab for suggestions on formatting e.g., callouts, heading levels, etc. to maintain some semblance of consistency among lesson authors!


Changing the lesson locally does not affect the lesson in the {lhLessons} package… (but see compare_diffs() and checkin_lessons() for more on that!). Any changes remain local, and will be rendered on the course site when those changes are committed and pushed.


1.2 Changing or adding images
For each lesson that already has images, there is a corresponding folder in the images folder. For example, if the course uses the git_setup lesson, there will be a folder images/git_setup/ where all the images for that lesson are stored. If you want to change an image (e.g., replace with a better resolution version, or swap for a different image), replace that file in the corresponding folder, and if you change the filename, update the filename inside the Quarto document as well. Easy!
If you want to add a new image to a lesson, find the appropriate folder and put the image there, then edit the Quarto document to point toward the proper image location. Easy! NOTE: if you’re adding an image to a lesson that doesn’t currently have any images, you may need to create the corresponding image folder. It is important that the folder name match the lesson name exactly (minus the prefix sXX_ and extension .qmd).
If you want to remove an image, just edit the Quarto doc and remove the file from the corresponding images folder. If it’s the last image being removed, maybe delete the corresponding image folder? but not critical!






Note



Because each lesson file corresponds to one folder of images, any images that are shared across multiple lessons will end up being duplicated. Sure, it’s a little redundant, but it helps prevent conflicts where an image is changed for one lesson, but the new image is not correct for the other lesson.




1.3 Changing or adding slides, data, or resources
Similar to changing or adding images - if a lesson is already associated with lesson-specific data or slides, it will have a corresponding folder in the data, slides, or resources folder, yay! Follow the same steps as noted for images.

title: Modify or add lessons
text:
2 Rearranging lessons
Oh noes! You created the course but now realize the flow would work better if the lessons were in a different order! No worries, this is pretty easy.
First, the prefixes on the lesson files, e.g., s01_r_studio_server_setup.qmd do not determine the order of lessons - they just make it easy to see the files in order in a file browser. The only thing that determines lesson order is inside the _quarto.yml document. In the website sidebar, there is a section called contents: with the index.qmd as the first file, then lessons in order, possibly broken into modules. This is bracketed by # START SESSIONS and # END SESSIONS in the _quarto.yml. (Before lessons are set up, a # SESSION_LINKS placeholder between these markers is what setup_lessons() replaces with the lesson sequence.)
For example, contents for a very simple course might look like this:
<... other stuff ...>
    contents:
      - index.qmd # preface
      # START SESSIONS
      - section: "Day 1"
        contents:
        - s01_r_rstudio_server_setup.qmd
        - s02_git_setup.qmd
      - section: "Day 2"
        contents:
        - s03_github_introduction.qmd
      # END SESSIONS
<... other stuff ...>
To reorder, you can just move the corresponding file into its new position in the sequence, without changing its prefix (the filename still needs to match the file!). If you have defined modules, make sure the lesson sequence falls into the proper modules. For example, to move the GitHub intro lesson to just before the Git setup lesson, and move the Git setup to day 2:
    contents:
      - index.qmd # preface
      # START SESSIONS
      - section: "Day 1"
        contents:
        - s01_r_rstudio_server_setup.qmd
        - s03_github_introduction.qmd    ### moved up
      - section: "Day 2"
        contents:
        - s02_git_setup.qmd              ### moved down
      # END SESSIONS
If the mismatched sequence numbers bug you, feel free to edit them in the _quarto.yml doc and rename the corresponding files, but it is not functionally necessary.

title: Modify or add lessons
text:
3 Adding a new lesson
Adding a new lesson is easy too. Two steps:

Create (or modify a copy of) a lesson file and add content, including optional images/slides/data.
Add your new lesson into the _quarto.yml lesson sequence in the appropriate location.


3.1 Create/modify a lesson file with content
Create a new file, or copy an existing one.

Give the new file a name that follows the general naming scheme, and add a prefix sXX_ where XX is a two-digit number (this prefix is important - it’s a flag that other {lhCore} package functions use to identify lesson files). Note, as for resequencing a lesson, the actual numbers aren’t important except for housekeeping - the actual sequencing is done in the _quarto.yml step that follows.

Format-wise, have a yaml header with a title (this gets printed in the lesson sidebar menu and at the top).
Follow all the style guidelines for headers, callouts, etc. to keep consistency with existing lessons.
If you include local figures, data, or slides, go to the appropriate folder (‘images’, ‘slides’, ‘data’, ‘resources’ - create if not already present in the course root directory) and add a subfolder with the bare name of your lesson (remove the sXX_ prefix and .qmd extension). Put your auxiliary files in the subfolder, and link to them from your lesson Quarto file.



3.2 Add new lesson to course sequence
The _quarto.yml needs to be modified to include the new lesson, in the proper position within the course sequence. Simply edit the file and save it. Using the earlier simple course as an example, if you wanted to add a new lesson at the start of day 2 about setting up Git in VS Code, you’d create a file (in the previous step) called s04_git_vscode_setup.qmd and add it into the sequence (remember, the numbers in the file prefix don’t dictate the sequence of the course):
    contents:
      - index.qmd # preface
      # START SESSIONS
      - section: "Day 1"
        contents:
        - s01_r_rstudio_server_setup.qmd
        - s02_git_setup.qmd
      - section: "Day 2"
        contents:
        - s04_git_vscode_setup.qmd     ### New lesson added into sequence
        - s03_github_introduction.qmd
      # END SESSIONS

title: Modify or add lessons
text:
4 Reorganizing the whole lesson sequence
If you wish to scrap the existing lesson sequence and restructure with new lessons, a different order, etc. you can use setup_lessons(..., overwrite = TRUE) with a new vector or dataframe defining a new lesson sequence.






Warning



overwrite = TRUE is destructive. After confirmation, it deletes all existing lesson .qmd files (sXX_*.qmd) and the matching lesson folders in images, data, slides, and resources, and then installs the new lessons. Any local edits or customizations to those lessons, including lessons you added yourself that follow the sXX_ naming, will be permanently lost. Commit your work to Git first, and consider running compare_diffs() and checkin_lessons() (see Compare changes and check in lessons) to preserve changes worth keeping.

title: Compare changes and check in lessons
text: Once a class has been taught, it is common for many, if not all, of the lessons to have been modified by the instructor. Many of these changes are simply typo fixes, others may contain more substantial changes to the content of the lesson, still others may implement new ideas about curriculum and pedagogy. Embedded in all these changes are improvements to the lesson, at least in the instructor’s eye. Being able to compare these changes to other versions of the lesson, discussing the merits and reasoning for changes among the Learning Hub staff, and incorporating the best improvements back into the lessons package will ensure the Learning Hub curriculum continues to improve.
crumbs: Compare changes and check in lessons

title: Compare changes and check in lessons
text:
1 Comparing with compare_diffs()
To compare differences between the course version of a lesson and its counterpart in the lessons package, open the course R project and use the compare_diffs() function. Its arguments are:

pkg - the lessons package (default "lhLessons").
org - the GitHub organization (or user) where the package lives (default "nceas-learning-hub").
pkg_version - optional version to compare against: a tag, commit, or version as accepted by the ref argument of remotes::install_github(). If both pkg_version and branch are given, pkg_version is used.
branch - optional branch to compare against. If both this and pkg_version are NULL, the default branch of the lessons repository is looked up on GitHub (it is not assumed to be main).
prefix - the expected prefix letter of lesson files (default "s", as in s01_).
file_out - name of the text file, saved in the project root, where the diff results are written (default git_diff.txt).

The function installs the lessons package fresh from GitHub into a temporary library (removed afterwards), so the comparison never depends on which version you happen to have installed. It compares every sXX_ lesson file in the course (there is no argument to restrict the comparison to selected lessons) to the lesson of the same bare name in the package, using git diff. It returns (invisibly) a dataframe with columns file_remote, file_local, result (the Git rundown of added/deleted lines), and status (0 = no difference, 1 = changed, 2 = new lesson not found in the package). Note that file_remote points into the temporary library, which no longer exists once the function returns. Messages list the files with changes and the new files detected, and a warning is issued for lessons that appear to be new.
A few things to be aware of:

Lessons are matched on bare name (e.g., s02_git_setup.qmd is compared to git_setup.qmd). If a lesson file was renamed (beyond the prefix), it is assumed to be a new lesson and is not compared.
Changes to auxiliary files (images, slides, data) are not compared, though changes to the paths of these files inside the lesson file will show up.
crumbs: Compare changes and check in lessons

title: Compare changes and check in lessons
text:
2 Checking in with checkin_lessons()
Ideally, the course instructor would then present these changes to the rest of the Learning Hub staff to decide which changes to keep and which to drop. If all agree that the changes are worth keeping, the instructor can then continue with the checkin_lessons() function. If there are disagreements, the instructor can modify the lessons (or exclude certain lessons) to address any questions or concerns of other Learning Hub staff.
Once changes have been reviewed, these changes (or a subset) can be pushed back to the lessons repository using the checkin_lessons() function. Its arguments are:

lessons - which lessons to check in. This can be NULL (default; all sXX_ lessons in the course), a character vector of lesson names (with or without the prefix and .qmd extension), or the dataframe returned by compare_diffs(), in which case only lessons with changes or new lessons (status != 0) are checked in.
pkg - the lessons package, i.e., the name of its GitHub repository (default "lhLessons").
org - the GitHub organization where the repository lives (default "nceas-learning-hub").
branch - the branch to push to. The default (NULL) uses the course project name (the name of the project root folder).

The function first asks the instructor to confirm they are in the right course project, lists the lessons to be checked in, and asks for confirmation. It then clones the lessons repository to a temporary location (not the installed package), checks out the branch (creating it if it doesn’t exist), and copies over the lesson files plus any associated slides, data, images, and resources folders. The staged changes are listed, and the instructor is asked once more to confirm before the function commits, pulls, and pushes to GitHub. If there are no differences from the repository, the function stops with an error.
At that point, the instructor can (assuming code review is complete) merge the changes from the course-specific branch back to the main branch.






ExampleExample






diffs <- compare_diffs()
checkin_lessons(diffs)

title: Content guidelines
text:
There are some tricks to getting Quarto to display certain information in a helpful way, especially around code. This document outlines some of those tricks to control how Quarto displays/executes code (or doesn’t, as the lesson requires).
See https://cambiotraining.github.io/quarto-course-template/materials/02-content_guidelines.html for ideas.
See also the style guide for suggestions on text case, learning objectives, code chunks, tabsets, images, links, and callout customization.

title: Content guidelines
text:
1 Headers and such
The lesson’s title in the YAML header is rendered as the page title (the top-level heading), and the site numbers sections automatically, so in the body of the lesson:

Do not use a single-# heading; start with ## for the main sections of the lesson. (The existing lessons overwhelmingly follow this pattern.)
Use ### and #### for subsections and sub-subsections. Try not to go deeper than four levels.
Don’t type numbers into headings; they are added automatically.
Keep headings short and descriptive, since they populate the table of contents in the right sidebar.
Don’t skip levels (e.g., a #### directly under a ##).


1.1 YAML header
Each lesson needs a title, which is shown in the sidebar menu and at the top of the page. Lessons in the lessons package also commonly include:

categories: a list of topic tags, e.g., categories: [r-basics, lecture, beginner]. These are what the tags argument of search_lessons() matches against, so reuse existing tags where possible.
description: a one-sentence summary of the lesson.

---
title: Working in R & RStudio
categories: [r-basics, lecture, beginner]
description: "RStudio basics, running code in the Console and scripts, ..."
---


1.2 Learning objectives
Open each lesson with a block listing learning objectives, using a {.callout-learning} div (“By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: …”). The theme gives this callout a green style, a brain icon, and the title “Learning Objectives”.
Write it like this, placed right after the YAML header:
:::{.callout-learning}

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

-   Navigate the basics of the RStudio interface
-   Run code and basic arithmetic in the Console
-   Use the Help pages to look up function documentation
:::
which will render like:






LearningLearning Objectives






By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

Navigate the basics of the RStudio interface
Run code and basic arithmetic in the Console
Use the Help pages to look up function documentation

title: Content guidelines
text:
2 Code formatting

code that needs to be run, identical to what we want to show the reader: just write it in a regular R code chunk, and make sure echo is not set to FALSE.
code that needs to be run, but is different than we want to show the reader, e.g., reading in a file from a different source than presented in the lesson: #| include: false - this lets the chunk execute, but conceals the code. If you want the reader to see different code, use a non-executing code chunk - one of the options below.
code that doesn’t need to be run: enclose in code block fence with language name next to it for syntax highlighting (e.g., ```r instead of in curly braces ```{r} used for a functioning code block!).
code that should not execute but you want to show the code chunk header and footer along with the code, begin with a double-curly-bracket r in the header: ```{{r}}. Use this when you want to show the reader how to write an actual code chunk, possibly including options in the header portion.
optional, use footnotes by including # <1> at the end of a line, then a 1. footnote text here immediately after the code chunk (similar for # <2> etc.). This works in functional code or non-functional code!







ExampleExample






Example of a footnote in a non-executing code chunk that includes R syntax highlighting:
```r
x <- 3 * 4 # <1>
```
1. This is an example of a footnote!
will render like:
1x <- 3 * 4

1

This is an example of a footnote!












ExampleExample






Example of a code chunk (non-executing) that shows the header/footer backticks and curly-braced r.
```{{r code-chunk-name-or-whatever}}
x <- 3 * 4 
```

will render (but NOT execute) like:
```{r code-chunk-name-or-whatever}
x <- 3 * 4 
```

title: Content guidelines
text:
3 Callouts
Quarto offers some built-in callout blocks to set content off against the normal body text. Note that we’ve customized the colors of our callouts to better match our course styling (see the nceas-learning-hub/theme extension in _extensions).

3.1 Standard callouts
There are five built-in callouts signalling different levels of urgency:

tip {.callout-tip}
note {.callout-note}
caution {.callout-caution}
warning {.callout-warning}
important {.callout-important}

See the callout reference for how to create these.
Based on the color and icons, here are recommendations on when and how to use these, in descending order of urgency:






Important



Use {.callout-important} to highlight things that the reader must pay attention to, or essential ideas and concepts.








Warning



Use {.callout-warning} to highlight common “gotchas” such as common user errors or unexpected behavior.








Caution



Use {.callout-caution} to indicate materials under development; consider using {.callout-warning} for other cases.








Note



Use {.callout-note} to communicate deeper ideas or understandings that are not critical to understanding the lesson at hand. The instructor might skip over these while teaching. If the reader does not read this, they may miss out, but nothing bad will happen.








Tip



Use {.callout-tip} to communicate key points and helpful tips and tricks. (Learning objectives have their own callout; see above.)




3.2 Custom callouts
There are currently five custom callouts for different types of content:

exercise {.callout-exercise}
hint {.callout-hint}
answer {.callout-answer}
example {.callout-example}
learning objectives {.callout-learning} (see above)

These custom callouts work thanks to Tavares, H., van Rongen, M., Cardona, A. (2024). Course Development Guidelines. https://cambiotraining.github.io/quarto-course-template/. Unfortunately, the title is not responsive to the title argument in the callout or to the header-style titling that the built-in callouts can use. The collapse option also seems to be unresponsive currently.






ExerciseExercise






Use {.callout-exercise} for exercises. The current default numbers exercises within a given page. Click on the hint and answer callouts below to reveal the information in them.






HintHint






Use {.callout-hint} for hints to the exercise - defaults to collapse=true for obvious reasons. Note they can be nested within an exercise, or stand-alone.










AnswerAnswer






Use {.callout-answer} for answers to the exercise - defaults to collapse=true for obvious reasons. Note they can be nested within an exercise, or stand-alone.














ExampleExample






Use {.callout-example} for examples, e.g., example data or example.

title: The {lhCore} package
text:
Course development with {lhCore}
The {lhCore} package and its sister package, {lhLessons}, were developed to make it easy for a course designer/instructor to set up a course using materials from the NCEAS Learning Hub.






NoteTo install:



You will need to install both {lhCore} (for functionality) and {lhLessons} (for content):
remotes::install_github('nceas-learning-hub/lhCore')
remotes::install_github('nceas-learning-hub/lhLessons')

title: The {lhCore} package
text:
1 What does {lhCore} do?
The {lhCore} package has a few key functions:

init_course() initializes a course by setting up a new repository, including a style template and Quarto website structure, sets up the repository for Git/GitHub functionality, and sets up automatic publication to GitHub Pages.
setup_lessons() copies selected lessons from the {lhLessons} package into the course repository and sets up the structure of the course as a Quarto website.







Note



The {lhCore} functions that create or change a course (init_course(), setup_lessons(), update_lessons(), checkin_lessons()) are designed to be run interactively, from the R console, because they ask for confirmation along the way. Running them from a script or other non-interactive session produces an error (unless the option lhCore.allow_noninteractive is set to TRUE).


Additional functions to help with setting up a course:

update_lessons() will update lessons (or revert to older ones) based on instructor selection of a version of the {lhLessons} package.
search_lessons() provides available lesson names (searchable by name or by topic tag) based on the installed version of the {lhLessons} package.
compare_diffs() identifies differences between the course versions of lessons and the parent lessons in the lhLessons repository, e.g., edits made while teaching the course or new lessons created for the course.
checkin_lessons() allows the instructor to push edited and new lessons back to the lhLessons repository, in a branch specific to the instructor’s course. The updates in the branch can then be merged with the main branch through a code review process.

title: The {lhCore} package
text:
2 What does {lhLessons} do?
The {lhLessons} package has essentially no user-facing functionality (just a couple of minor helper functions), but instead houses lessons as Quarto documents, along with templates and support files to construct a course. Why is this separate from {lhCore}?

First, it seemed like a good idea to allow the course lesson content to be version-controlled separately from the package containing the functions.

Second, this allows for other instructors or organizations to create their own lesson content or structure that can play nicely with the {lhCore} functionality - for example, if the curriculum for the Delta Stewardship Council diverged from the {lhCore} curriculum, we could create a {deltaLessons} package to contain different content, and even a different style or format.

Third, it allows an instructor to choose different versions of the content and perhaps update an old course, if the materials for the old course are significantly out of date, using GitHub release tags that refer to different versions of the content related to specific points in time.

title: The {lhCore} package
text:
3 Why {lhCore}?

3.1 Where we’re at
For years NCEAS has been offering courses through the Learning Hub, the Arctic Data Center, the Delta Stewardship Council, and working group workshops, among other efforts. The course offerings include lessons on collaboration with Git and GitHub, reproducibility with R and RStudio, and fundamental techniques of working with all kinds of data. As of October 2024, these courses have been built in the nceas-training repository of the NCEAS GitHub organization, with each course built on a separate branch. These courses are rendered by GitHub actions set up in the repro-research-course repository, where the courses are linked to an NCEAS URL, and archived in the repo.
This system has worked for years, and the lesson offerings have grown organically over time to over a hundred different .Rmds and .qmds. But setting up a new course is tricky - after establishing a desired curriculum, an instructor needs to manually identify relevant lessons from a long list of files with inconsistent file naming, and then needs to manually set up files to link to these lessons, all within a new branch to avoid affecting other lessons (and to work with the Github actions to publish the course). The lesson catalog contains duplicates, updated versions, deprecated lessons, etc. The instructor then frequently has to make edits to the lessons, on that separate branch. As of this writing, there are 43 separate branches, each likely holding improvements and valuable edits, with no well defined process to thoughtfully incorporate the best of those ideas into the latest and greatest versions of each lesson.


3.2 Where we’re going
By setting up a new NCEAS Learning Hub organization, and designing the {lhCore} and {lhLessons} packages, we can accomplish a few things:

Make it far easier to set up a typical Learning Hub training by automating and streamlining many of the setup steps.
Curate the course offerings and try to outline some standards for adding additional course offerings, for consistency.
Use distinct repositories to host each course, rather than branches all held within a single repository. This seems more in line with how we teach the use of Git and GitHub.
Update course lessons so that old course offerings can be brought into line with current course offerings (or lessons can be reverted to old versions).
Use GitHub Pages to easily and automatically publish courses to the web.
Facilitate post-course review of edits and updates to course materials, to better share wisdom and ideas across the various spokes of the NCEAS Learning Hub.

title: Publishing Synthesis Data
text:
1 Overview
Imagine you are conducting a synthesis project relating stream environmental conditions to ecological outcomes over a 50-year historical period. You’ll likely need data collected by multiple federal agencies, various state and regional authorities, university researchers who manage relevant labs and programs, and other organizations such as local watershed coalitions and non-profit groups. Some of the data you can find immediately; some requires sending email requests for datasets that, if you’re lucky, you eventually receive via email attachments with minimal documentation; some of it you’re never able to access – or perhaps it was never permanently saved in the first place.
Despite tremendous improvements in recent decades, this is still the current reality of environmental data, and it is an obstacle to science. The practices in this session are how we change it.
This module covers data documentation, publication, and sharing: why it matters, where data should live, what makes data truly reusable, and how to evaluate data publications using a principled framework. You can – and should! – view this from the perspective of both a consumer and producer. After all, as you work on your own data-oriented project, you will almost certainly generate new data products that you should make available for others in the spirit of open and collaborative science.

title: Creating R Packages
text:
1 Overview
Most R users are familiar with loading and using packages in their work; we’ve worked with a number of well-known packages in this course thus far! In addition, even if they mostly stick to a core set of packages, they understand the breadth of packages available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (a.k.a. “CRAN”; the R package authority) for handling virtually any conceivable need. However, most R users have never created a package for their own work, often out of a fear that the process is too complicated. In reality, it’s fairly straighforward and super useful in your personal work. Creating packages serves two main use-cases:

Distribute reusable code among projects (even if just for yourself)
Reproducibly document analysis and models and their results

Even if you don’t plan on writing a package with such broad appeal such as, say, ggplot2 or dplyr, you still might consider creating a package to contain:

Useful utility functions you write (i.e., a Personal Package)

Having a place to put these functions makes it much easier to find and use them later.

A set of shared routines for your lab or research group, making it easier to remain consistent within your team and also to save time.
The analysis accompanying a thesis or manuscript, making it all that much easier for others to reproduce your results.
